overfit.key_finding: FLOOR vs COLLAPSE, and it is COLLAPSE. gr00t-n15 showed the framing 'ACT's arm is worse than do-nothing' is weighting-dependent (frame-weighted margin -0.1404 flips to +0.0029 episode-equal -- reproduced here exactly), so that gap is simply unresolved. The question that survives reweighting is whether ACT's arm sits at do-nothing level because the architecture cannot do better (floor) or because it fails to transfer (collapse). On TRAIN the arm beats hold by +1.4778 frame-weighted / +1.5203 episode-equal -- 2.3x better than do-nothing under BOTH calibers -- while on val it is indistinguishable from do-nothing under both. A floor would hold on train too. It does not: ACT's arm CAN represent this task and does not transfer.

split_difficulty_control.why: openvla-oft's rider: a train/val gap is not overfit evidence until the two splits' INTRINSIC DIFFICULTY difference is subtracted
split_difficulty_control.method: constant (image-blind) predictors, pure numpy, no model and no GPU -- scripts/lerobot_split_difficulty.py. Reported at FULL population (7475 train / 1397 val): these predictors cost nothing to evaluate, so there is no reason to run them on the model's 400-anchor subsample.
split_difficulty_control.verdict: At full population the pure-difficulty null is 0.9989 -- val is 0.11% EASIER -- so intrinsic difficulty explains essentially NONE of the train/val gap; the whole ratio is the model's. My earlier '2.3% of the gap' was itself a 400-anchor artifact. Sharpest evidence that the subsampling default was the defect: a MODEL-FREE constant predictor moves 2.4% between the n=400 draw (1.0226) and the population (0.9989) -- no weights, no RNG, no GPU, so only sampling can have moved it.
split_difficulty_control.note_hold_direction: The 400-anchor hold ratio 0.930 read as 'val is much easier in DELTA space'; at full population it is 0.9974, so that effect was almost entirely sampling. The general point survives and is worth keeping: hold-state is a DELTA-flavoured proxy, so match the proxy to the row's parameterization -- const-abs for an absolute leg.
split_difficulty_control.anchor_construction_is_uniform_in_time: stride 5, drop last K per episode -- anchors are proportional to episode length in BOTH splits, so oft's 'per-episode N dilutes long episodes differently' cannot arise by construction; val rebuild asserted bit-exact vs frozen val_anchors.npz
split_difficulty_control.free_byproduct_split_is_not_adversarial: const-abs fitted on TRAIN vs on each split's own anchors differ by <1.1% (train 20.9949 vs 20.9359, val 21.6432 vs 21.4090) => the two splits' marginal action distributions are near-identical; holds board-wide

overfit.subsample_caveat: EVERY number in overfit.train / overfit.val -- INCLUDING BOTH HOLD LINES -- is a 400-anchor draw. lerobot_train_split_eval.py's --n defaulted to 400 (openvla-oft caught it; default is now 0=ALL and a subset prints a WARNING). Measured cost: ACT's val MAE has sd 0.063 over 400-anchor draws (95% +-0.124); the seed-0 draw read 2.6665 against the full-1397 truth 2.7272, so the ratio inherits ~+-0.13 -- the same order as real gaps between backbones. The DIRECTION of the overfit finding is unaffected (2.14 is nowhere near 1.0) but 2.141 must NOT be compared digit-for-digit against another leg's ratio. Full-population re-run is pending a GPU window.

overfit.scope: FULL POPULATION both splits (--n 0). No subsampling, no draw, no seed.
overfit.weighting: frame-length-weighted: unweighted mean over anchors, so a long episode contributes proportionally more anchors. BOTH splits in the same caliber. Episode-equal caliber also computed -- see weighting_robustness below.

ratio_se.method: delete-one-EPISODE jackknife per split + delta method for the ratio of means over two disjoint clustered samples; cross-checked by a pooled union jackknife (agrees to <2%)

SUPERSEDED_n400_numbers.why: --n defaulted to 400, silently narrowing the statistical population. Every number in this block was a single 400-anchor draw. The ratio moved 2.141 -> 2.301 (+7.5%) at full population, i.e. the subsample biased the overfit DOWNWARD.

weighting_robustness.why: gr00t-n15 measured that per-frame -> per-episode reweighting is a DETERMINISTIC shift (not sampling noise) which moves numerator and denominator in OPPOSITE directions (corr(ep length, model MAE) +0.34 vs corr(ep length, hold MAE) -0.62), so any model-vs-hold quantity must be shown in a stated caliber.
weighting_robustness.verdict: The OVERFIT RATIO is caliber-robust: 2.301 frame-weighted vs 2.260 episode-equal (TOTAL), 2.305 vs 2.257 (ARM), 2.275 vs 2.280 (GRIP) -- all shifts are well inside the +-0.12 episode-jackknife SE. What is NOT caliber-robust is the cross-model arm-vs-hold margin on val, which changes sign. Both facts have the same cause and opposite consequences: reweighting moves a SMALL difference of two similar numbers, and leaves a 2.3x RATIO alone.
weighting_robustness.independent_reproduction: episode-equal val arm margin +0.0029 vs hold reproduces gr00t-n15's independently computed +0.0029 exactly (different code, different stack, same frozen anchors)

preds_write_gate.guard: lerobot_predict.py refuses to write preds_*.npz if the K=8 prefix has any non-finite cell
preds_write_gate.why: gr00t-n15 measured a NaN row misorders the WHOLE board (score.py's mae>=HOLD_MAE is False for NaN; a NaN sort key breaks Timsort transitivity); gr00t-n17 hit a variant where a NaN SE fell into an `else inf` branch and printed RESOLVED. Every new consumer that globs preds/ needs its own ingestion gate -- a write-side gate makes the bad file not exist.
preds_write_gate.scoped_to_K: checks pred[:, :K, :] only, so it cannot false-fire on padding past the scoring window
